segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also came to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple named Timothy was there, the son of a believing Jewish woman but of a Greek father,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he was well spoken of by the brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul wanted this man to set out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they traveled through the cities, they handed on to them the decrees decided on by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to keep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith and grew in number day by day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came up to Mysia, they tried to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: During the night a vision appeared to Paul: a Macedonian man was standing there, pleading with him and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to bring the good news to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we put out to sea from Troas and ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of that district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city for some days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God, was listening, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When she and her household had been baptized, she pleaded with us, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And she prevailed on us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Once, as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl who had a spirit of divination met us. She brought her owners a great deal of profit by fortune-telling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She followed after Paul and us, crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These men are slaves of the Most High God, and they are proclaiming to you a way of salvation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She kept doing this for many days. But Paul, exasperated, turned and said to the spirit,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to go out of her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it went out that very hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and bringing them to the magistrates they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These men are throwing our city into turmoil; they are Jews,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and they are proclaiming customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowd joined in the attack on them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison, commanding the jailer to guard them securely.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having received such a command, he threw them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the jail were shaken. At once all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains came loose.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The jailer woke up, and seeing the doors of the prison open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul called out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The jailer asked for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he brought them outside and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds, and he and all who were his were baptized at once.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He brought them up into his house and set a meal before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household that he had come to believe in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Release those men.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The jailer reported these words to Paul:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So come out now and go in peace.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They beat us in public without a trial, men who are Romans, and threw us into prison, and now they are throwing us out in secret? No indeed! Let them come themselves and bring us out.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they came and pleaded with them, and after bringing them out they kept asking them to leave the city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After coming out of the prison they went to Lydia’s house, and when they had seen the brothers and sisters they encouraged them and departed.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it means the members of the believing community. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; several recent ones use “brothers and sisters” or “believers.” In verse 40 the group meets in Lydia’s house and plainly includes women.

The verb is the ordinary word for handing something into another’s keeping, and it is also used for passing on teaching or instructions. Most versions have “delivered”; “handed on” keeps the link with the same verb elsewhere. The “decrees” are the decisions of the Jerusalem meeting in the previous chapter.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used of civic assemblies and, in the Greek Old Testament, of Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible wherever it appears.

notes.traditional: Phrygia and the region of Galatia
notes.note: The Greek can be read as one district (the part of Phrygia lying within the Roman province of Galatia) or as two (Phrygia, and Galatian territory farther north). The choice bears on the long-running debate over where the Galatian assemblies were, and scholars remain divided. “Asia” here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, not the continent.

Here the narrative shifts without explanation from “they” to “we,” the first of several such passages in Acts. The usual explanation is that the author, or a source he used, joined Paul’s party at Troas; some scholars regard the first-person plural as a literary convention. The “we” drops away after Philippi and resumes in chapter 20.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and a book title, so this translation uses “good news.” Many modern versions already alternate between the two.

notes.phrase: a leading city of that district of Macedonia
notes.traditional: the chief city of that part of Macedonia
notes.note: The text translated is the reading of the principal manuscripts. It is awkward historically, since Philippi was the capital neither of the province nor of its own district, and so some editions adopt a conjecture, “a city of the first district of Macedonia.” Macedonia had been divided into four districts by the Romans. “A leading city” takes the Greek as a claim to prominence and not to capital status.

Luke uses the Latin word in Greek letters. A Roman colony was a settlement, often of army veterans, whose citizens held Roman citizenship and lived under Roman law and Roman-style magistrates. This explains the accusers’ appeal in verse 21 to what is lawful “for us” as Romans.

The Greek word for “prayer” was also a regular term for a Jewish meeting place, sometimes a building and sometimes an open-air site, often near water. The fact that only women are mentioned may suggest that Philippi had no established synagogue. Some manuscripts read “where prayer was customarily offered.”

In Acts this expression regularly describes Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue and worshiped Israel’s God without becoming full converts. Lydia was probably such a person and not Jewish by birth. Thyatira, in the province of Asia, was known for its dyeing trade, and purple cloth was a luxury product.

The Greek is literally “a spirit, a python.” Python was the serpent of Delphi in Greek myth, slain by Apollo, whose oracle there was the most famous in the Greek world; by this period the word was used for a spirit believed to speak predictions through a person, and for such soothsayers themselves. A first-century reader would have understood that the girl was regarded as an oracle.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and not for a hired servant. Most translations soften it to “servants.” In the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and the prophets. The word is pointed on the lips of a girl who is herself owned.

The Greek has no article, so the phrase can be read as “a way” or “the way” of salvation. “Most High God” was a title Jews used for the God of Israel, but Gentiles also used it for Zeus or another supreme deity, and “salvation” could mean rescue or well-being of many kinds. To a crowd in Philippi the girl’s cry was therefore open to a pagan understanding, which may be part of why Paul is exasperated.

The Greek word, literally “generals,” was the standard Greek equivalent for the pair of chief magistrates who governed a Roman colony. They are probably the same officials as “the authorities” in verse 19, now named by their title.

The jailer’s respectful address is the plural of the word translated “Lord” in the reply of verse 31 and “owners” in verses 16 and 19. A Greek reader would have heard the echo: he addresses them as lords, and they point him to the Lord Jesus.

The Greek word means “rod-bearers” and was the regular term for Roman lictors, the attendants who walked before a magistrate carrying a bundle of rods as the sign of his authority and who carried out his sentences. The verb for “beaten with rods” in verse 22 is from the same root, so these are presumably the men who did the beating. “Police” suggests a modern institution that did not exist.

“Romans” here means holders of Roman citizenship, not natives of Rome. Roman law protected citizens from being beaten or imprisoned without trial, and officials who violated that protection could face serious consequences, which explains the magistrates’ fear in verse 38. There is irony in the charge of verse 21, where the accusers set themselves as Romans against Paul and Silas as Jews.

candidates.reason: The plural for community members recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translations split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
“Slave” versus “servant” affects hundreds of verses, including Paul’s self-designations and the parables, and needs one policy.
The verb ranges over urge, plead, encourage, comfort and conciliate, and the choice of English per sense should be fixed across books.
The split between “house” and “household” matters in the household-baptism passages and should be consistent across Acts and the letters.
The participle is a semi-technical label in Acts for Gentile adherents of the synagogue and needs a uniform rendering alongside φοβούμενος τὸν θεόν.
